text: Thomas Randolph (1523–1590) was an English ambassador to Elizabeth I of England and spent much of his professional life in Scotland, serving at the courts of Mary, Queen of Scots, and her son James VI. He was involved in marriage negotiations and various political upheavals. Between 1568 and 1569, he was sent on a special mission to Russia, where he visited the court of Ivan the Terrible and secured privileges for English merchants, leading to the formation of the Muscovy Company. Randolph served as a Member of Parliament for New Romney in 1558, Maidstone in 1584, 1586, and 1589, Grantham in 1559, St Ives in 1558 and 1572. Born in 1523 to Avery Randolph of Badlesmere, Kent, and Anne Gainsford (not the lady-in-waiting to Anne Boleyn), he entered Christ Church, Oxford at its foundation, graduated with a B.A. in October 1545 and a B.C.L. in 1548, became a public notary, and was principal of Broadgates Hall (now Pembroke College), Oxford until 1553. Due to Protestant persecutions under Queen Mary, he resigned and retired to France, where he resided in Paris and was influenced by George Buchanan, whom he praised in a letter to Peter Young, tutor of James VI. Among his fellow students in Paris was Sir William Kirkcaldy of Grange. After Elizabeth's accession in 1558, Randolph acted as an agent in Germany before returning to England and purchasing a farm in Kent—the house where he was born. His knowledge of Scottish Protestants in Paris led Elizabeth to employ him in bringing the Earl of Arran from Geneva to England. He sometimes signed his letters with the Latin phrase "Virtus pro divitiis," which he wrote in a copy of John Jewel's Apologia ecclesiae Anglicanae (1562), now held by the University of Edinburgh. Under the name Barnabie and using the codename Pamphilus, he was sent in autumn 1559 to secretly transport James Hamilton, 3rd Earl of Arran, into Scotland. He returned to London on 25 November but was again sent to Scotland in March 1560, where his efforts influenced Protestant opposition to the queen-regent and helped establish an understanding with Elizabeth. His continued role as a confidential agent for Elizabeth, and also for William Cecil, the secretary of state, gave him significant influence in Scottish politics despite lacking diplomatic skill compared to Maitland of Lethington. His numerous letters remain vital sources on the Queen of Scots' court, political plots, and social intrigues. At the marriage of Lord James Stewart and Agnes Keith in February 1562, Mary toasted Elizabeth from a gold cup and presented it to Randolph, discussing the "amity" between England and Scotland; Mary was also sent a portrait of Elizabeth, which Randolph verified. In autumn 1562, Randolph accompanied Mary on a northern expedition that resulted in the defeat and death of George Gordon, 4th Earl of Huntly, and he participated in the campaign, stating he was "ashamed to sit still where so many were occupied." In January 1563, he attended the wedding of James Stewart, Commendator of Inchcolm, and Margaret Campbell at Castle Campbell, describing feasts, banqueting, masking, and running at the ring. In June 1563, he met a servant of Catholic priest John Black at St Andrews, bribed him to reveal correspondence, and copied it. On 5 June 1563, Elizabeth granted him a license to return to England for private business. In April 1563, he was sent to Scotland to entangle Mary in marriage negotiations with Lord Robert Dudley, Elizabeth's favourite; initially unenthusiastic, Mary eventually accepted the proposal after Elizabeth declared her official heir on the condition of marriage. In September 1564, Elizabeth granted Dudley the earldom of Leicester to improve his appeal, and in early 1565, Mary accepted the match. However, Dudley refused to marry Mary and showed passive resistance, which Randolph repeatedly tried to overcome through letters. Elizabeth later withdrew her support for the succession declaration. When Henry Stuart, Lord Darnley, became a serious candidate, Elizabeth sought to prevent the marriage, and Randolph received instructions to push for a union with Dudley or another noble; if the proposal was irreversible, he was to report how it would distress her. Randolph reported on a Roman antiquity discovered near Edinburgh at Musselburgh, including an inscribed altar and hypocaust, and courted Mary Beaton, one of Mary's companions. In April 1565, Beaton and Randolph played bowls at Stirling Castle with the queen and Darnley, winning and receiving a ring and brooch worth fifty crowns from Darnley. A letter from Alexander Clark mocked their relationship with nonsense words: "And as to your mistress Marie Beton, she is both darimpus and sclenbrunit, and you in like manner without contrebaxion or kylteperante, so you are both worth little money." Randolph failed to prevent Mary's marriage to Darnley and declined to recognize Darnley's authority. His representations may have contributed to the rebellion of James Stewart, 1st Earl of Moray, known as the Chaseabout Raid. On 16 January 1566, he reported that Mary had withheld the "Matrimonial crown" from Darnley and was now pregnant, noting she felt the movement on New Year's Day and had milk in her breasts. On 14 February 1566, he wrote to the Earl of Leicester that he could not commit to writing about Mary's actions due to fear of appearing "malicieus foolyshe and unadvised." In February 1566, Mary accused him of aiding Moray and her rebels with a gift of three thousand crowns, requiring him to leave the country within six days. He retired to Berwick upon Tweed, where after Riccio's murder, he was accused of writing a book against Mary called Mr. Randolph's Phantasy. He was recalled to England around June 1566 and appointed "Master of the King's Post," later becoming postmaster general. On 2 November 1567, he obtained from Robert Constable an assignment as constable of Queenborough Castle and steward of the manor of Middleton and Merden in Kent. In June 1568, he was sent to Russia to support English merchants, securing privileges from Ivan IV that led to the Muscovy Company's formation; he returned in autumn 1569. Following representations by Regent Moray's agent Nicolas Elphinstone in January 1570, he was sent to Scotland despite uncertain news of Moray's assassination. He remained in Scotland for a year. In October 1573 and April 1576, he conducted special embassies to France. In February 1578, he was sent to Scotland but too late to prevent the fall of James Douglas, 4th Earl of Morton. After Morton's imprisonment in 1580, he returned to Scotland to negotiate on his behalf. At a convention of the estates on 20 February 1581, he presented a paper on the Queen's intentions and offers to the King of Scotland and delivered a two-hour speech denouncing Esme Stewart, created Duke of Lennox, as a Roman agent. His bold action only sealed Morton's fate. He then attempted, with Elizabeth's approval, to plot the seizure of Lennox and the young king, but the plot was betrayed, and he fled to Berwick after narrowly escaping death from a shot fired in the provost's house in Edinburgh. His advice directly influenced English policy, advising Elizabeth against military intervention in Scotland against the Lennox government. In January 1586, he was sent on his final mission to Scotland with Thomas Mills to negotiate a treaty between England and Scotland, which he successfully secured through the signature of James VI despite opposition from French diplomat Charles de Prunelé, Baron d'Esneval. In August 1586, Randolph and the Scottish ambassador Archibald Douglas sent male deer and huntsmen to James VI at Falkland Palace; the huntsmen likely included Cuthbert Rayne. He wrote: "I have sent the Kynge two hunting men, verie good and skillful, with one footman, that can hoop, hollow and crye, that all the trees in Fawkland will quake for fear. Pray the Kynge's Majestie to be mercifull to the poor bucks; but let him spare and look well to himself." He presented £4,000 to James VI from Elizabeth, the first regular subsidy, noting that James VI, like previous regents, did not issue receipts for such payments, explaining that princes avoid "bills of their hands" to prevent "danger or reproach." Randolph held the joint offices of Chamberlain of the Exchequer and Master of the Post until his death on 8 June 1590, at age sixty-seven, in his house on St. Peter's Hill, near Thames Street, London, and was buried in the church of St. Peter's, Paul's Wharf. Throughout his embassies, he was frequently short of money and struggled to pay expenses. Despite his significant services, he received no substantial reward beyond these modest offices. The claim that he was knighted in 1571 is not supported by evidence. He is believed to have authored the original short Latin Life of George Buchanan, though this is at least doubtful; he showed strong interest in Buchanan's History and offered financial support for its completion. In July 1593, the Scottish ambassador, with Roger Aston, claimed that Randolph had promised in 1586 to pay James VI an annual subsidy of £5,000, a claim William Cecil deemed unlikely and which prompted a search of Randolph's papers. In late 1571, he married Anne Walsingham, daughter of Thomas Walsingham of Chislehurst and cousin once removed of Francis Walsingham. Before the marriage, on 1 October 1571, he received letters patent from Thomas Walsingham and William Crowner granting custody of the manor and hundred of Middleton and Merden at a rent of 100 pounds per annum to be paid to his wife. In 1572, he was appointed Chamberlain of the Exchequer for life. His friend George Buchanan teased him about the marriage, saying: "If you had been in your right wit, you being once escaped the tempestous storms and naufrage (shipwreck) of marriage, had never entered again the same dangers, for I cannot take you for a Stoic philosopher, having one head inexpugnable (not to be captured) with the frenetic tortures of jealousy, or a careless heart sceptic that takes cuckoldry as thing indifferent." Their children included: Thomas Randolph married secondly Ursula Copinger, daughter of Henry Copinger of Allhallows Hoo, Kent, and Buxhall, Suffolk, and his wife Agnes, daughter of Thomas Jermyn (died 1552); their children are listed. Randolph died in 1590.
